paragraphs.title: Why the hypotheses matter
paragraphs.p: The integral test is not a rule for every function. It requires f to be continuous, positive, and decreasing.
The positivity matters because the proof uses increasing partial sums and area comparison. If signs change, cancellation can change the behavior.
The decreasing condition matters because the rectangles must consistently sit above or below the curve. If the function jumps up and down, the rectangle comparison can fail.
paragraphs.md: \text{Do not use the integral test until positivity and decreasing behavior have been checked.}

exercise.title: Why can an improper integral decide a positive series?

statement.p: The Integral Test compares rectangle sums with the area under a positive decreasing curve. In your own words, why do the series and the improper integral stand or fall together, and why must positivity and decreasing behavior be checked first?

hint.p: If the area is infinite, the rectangles sitting above the curve are infinite too. If the area is finite, the increasing partial sums are bounded above. Without a consistent above-or-below comparison, the picture fails.

subsection.title: Direct comparison
subsection.p: The harmonic series and the series \sum 1/k^2 now become measuring sticks.
If a positive series is smaller than a known convergent positive series, it must converge. If it is larger than a known divergent positive series, it must diverge.

note.p: for all sufficiently large k, and

subsection.p: The phrase “for all sufficiently large k” means that finitely many early terms do not matter. Changing, adding, or deleting finitely many terms can change the value of a convergent series, but it cannot change whether the series converges.

paragraphs.title: Why the test works
paragraphs.p: For positive series, partial sums increase. If every term of a_k is eventually no larger than the corresponding term of b_k, then the partial sums of a_k are eventually controlled by the partial sums of b_k, plus a finite starting amount.
A finite starting amount cannot cause divergence. The infinite tail decides.

exercise.title: Why do nonnegative terms leave only two possibilities?

statement.p: For a series with a_k\ge 0, the partial sums are increasing. In your own words, why does that force the series either to converge or to diverge to infinity, and why is there no room for oscillation?

hint.p: An increasing sequence either is trapped by a ceiling or keeps rising. Cancellation is what would have allowed bouncing, and there is none.

exercise.title: Why is comparison the central habit for positive series?

statement.p: Direct comparison uses an inequality. Limit comparison uses a finite positive ratio of leading behaviors. In your own words, why can a known convergent series pull a smaller positive series along with it, and why do two series that look alike for large k share the same fate?

hint.p: For nonnegative terms, boundedness of partial sums is the whole story. A smaller series cannot outrun a convergent ceiling, and a finite positive ratio means the two tails are comparable in both directions.

exercise.title: Why is p=1 the boundary for p-series?

statement.p: The series \sum 1/k^p converges when p>1 and diverges when p\le 1. In your own words, why is the harmonic series the dividing line, and why can a series with p just above 1 converge very slowly while one just below 1 diverges very slowly?

hint.p: The Integral Test reduces the question to the area under 1/x^p. That area is finite precisely when the exponent is large enough to beat the harmonic case.

note.title: What to remember
note.p: For positive series, comparison is the central habit.
When an unfamiliar positive series appears, compare it with one of these measuring sticks.
